title: South Asians Do Everything Right for Heart Health and Still Get Sick Earlier. A 2,700-Person Study Finally Explains Why.
excerpt: Northwestern researchers found elevated rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension in South Asian Americans by age 45 — despite healthier diets and lower alcohol use.
body:
South Asian adults in the United States report doing many of the right things for heart health — eating well, drinking less, and exercising at roughly the same levels as other groups. And yet, by age 45, they carry significantly higher rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension than white and Chinese Americans, and rates comparable to or higher than Black and Hispanic patients.

That is the central finding of a new study led by Northwestern Medicine researchers, published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association*. It is the most detailed investigation to date of when cardiovascular risk factors emerge in South Asian Americans — and its conclusions challenge everything the community has been told about prevention.

## The Study

The research drew on long-term data from 2,700 adults, tracking participants with heritage from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka alongside white, Black, Chinese, and Hispanic Americans. Researchers compared the prevalence of key cardiovascular risk factors — diabetes, prediabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, and obesity — while also measuring each group's self-reported lifestyle behaviours.

South Asian participants reported healthier diets, lower alcohol consumption, and comparable levels of physical activity. Despite this, they had some of the highest prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors among all groups studied.

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviours and clinical risk was surprising," said senior author Dr. Namratha Kandula, professor of general internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians."

## The Critical Window

Perhaps the study's most actionable finding is that the risk is already elevated by age 45 — decades before heart disease typically becomes a clinical emergency.

"We've known for decades that South Asians develop heart disease younger, but we didn't have data showing exactly when risk begins," Kandula said. "We've now identified a critical window in the 40s when risk is already high, but disease is still preventable."

This has enormous implications for screening. Current US guidelines recommend cholesterol screening starting at age 20, diabetes screening at 35, and blood pressure checks at regular intervals. But for South Asians, these timelines may already be too late to catch the problem early enough.

## Why Standard Guidelines May Not Apply

The study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that South Asians have a fundamentally different cardiometabolic profile than other populations. Several factors may explain why healthy behaviour alone is not enough.

**Genetic predisposition.** South Asians carry higher rates of insulin resistance, visceral adiposity — fat stored around internal organs rather than under the skin — and unfavourable lipid profiles at lower body mass index thresholds. The World Health Organization has acknowledged that BMI cut-offs for overweight and obesity may need to be lower for South Asian populations.

**Dietary complexity.** While South Asian diets are often rich in vegetables, lentils, and spices, they can also be high in refined carbohydrates — white rice, naan, and sugary desserts — that spike blood glucose. The quality of carbohydrate intake may matter more than total fat or calorie counts.

**Metabolic programming.** Emerging research suggests that maternal nutrition during pregnancy, birth weight, and early childhood diet can set metabolic trajectories that persist into adulthood. Many first-generation immigrants grew up with different nutritional environments than those available in the US.

## What the Diaspora Should Do

The message is not that healthy behaviour is futile — it unquestionably reduces risk. But it may not be sufficient on its own. For South Asian Americans, the study's authors recommend earlier and more aggressive screening for diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, ideally starting in the late 30s rather than waiting for standard guideline ages.

They also urge clinicians to apply South Asian-specific BMI thresholds. A South Asian patient with a BMI of 23 may carry the same metabolic risk as a white patient with a BMI of 27 or higher.

For NRIs in the US, Canada, and the UK, this study should prompt a practical conversation with primary care physicians. Push for comprehensive metabolic panels in your early 40s. Ask about insulin resistance, not just fasting glucose. Request a coronary artery calcium score if you have a family history. And recognise that doing everything right by the standard playbook may not be enough — your biology operates on different thresholds, and knowing that early enough to intervene is half the battle.

The paradox Kandula identified is not a reason for fatalism. It is a reason for precision — the kind of screening and intervention that meets South Asian bodies where they actually are, not where general population guidelines assume them to be.
